llm_extracted_info.main_contributions: The paper addresses the challenge of generalizing Transformer architectures to large graph-structured data, identifying two main deficiencies: (1) existing node sampling strategies are agnostic to graph characteristics and training process, leading to sub-optimal performance, and (2) most sampling methods focus on local neighbors, neglecting long-range dependencies. To overcome these, the authors propose a Hierarchical Graph Transformer with Adaptive Node Sampling (ANS-GT). Key contributions include formulating node sampling as an adversary bandit problem to adaptively select informative nodes, and introducing a hierarchical attention scheme with graph coarsening to capture both local and global dependencies efficiently. The method achieves state-of-the-art performance on various real-world datasets for node classification.
llm_extracted_info.methodology: The proposed ANS-GT method consists of two core components: Adaptive Node Sampling and Hierarchical Graph Attention. For Adaptive Node Sampling, the optimization of node selection is framed as an adversary bandit problem, where the Exp4.P method is modified to adaptively assign weights to different sampling heuristics (e.g., 1-hop neighbors, 2-hop neighbors, Personalized PageRank (PPR), and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)). A novel reward scheme is introduced, proportional to the attention weights and sampling probabilities, updating sampling strategies during training to favor more informative nodes. For Hierarchical Graph Attention, a dual attention mechanism is employed: fine-grained local attention uses the adaptive node sampling for local nodes, while coarse-grained global attention utilizes graph coarsening algorithms (e.g., Variational Neighborhoods) to group nodes into super-nodes, enabling interaction with sampled super-nodes to capture long-range dependencies. Additionally, global nodes with learnable features are incorporated for broader context. Proximity encoding is used for positional information, and the model follows the standard Transformer layer structure with Multi-Head Self-Attention and Feed-Forward Networks.
llm_extracted_info.experimental_setup: The effectiveness of ANS-GT was evaluated on nine benchmark datasets for semi-supervised node classification: Cora, CiteSeer, PubMed (citation graphs); Chameleon, Squirrel (Wikipedia graphs); Actor (co-occurrence graph); and WebKB datasets (Cornell, Texas, Wisconsin). Additionally, the method was tested on large-scale OGB datasets, ogbn-arxiv and ogbn-products. A 60%/20%/20% split for train-validation-test was used. Baselines included eight popular Graph Neural Networks (GCN, GAT, GraphSAGE, JKNet, APPNP, Geom-GCN, H2GCN, GPRGNN) and four state-of-the-art Graph Transformers (GT, SAN, Graphormer, Gophormer). Node classification accuracy was the primary evaluation metric. The models were trained using the AdamW optimizer with a learning rate scheduler and a 100-epoch warm-up stage on an NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU. Hyperparameters such as dropout rate, hidden dimension, number of layers, sampled nodes, super-nodes, global nodes, and data augmentations were carefully tuned using grid search.
llm_extracted_info.limitations: One limitation of this work is the introduction of more hyperparameters that require fine-tuning for optimal performance. Additionally, the adaptive node sampling mechanism, while beneficial, may potentially introduce biases in the node sampling process during training.
llm_extracted_info.future_research_directions: The authors suggest exploring other positional encoding methods, such as Laplacian eigenvectors, as their current framework is agnostic to the specific positional encoding scheme. More broadly, they express hope that this work will contribute to generalizing Transformer architectures to the graph domain and encourage the unified modeling of multi-modal data.

from numpy.linalg import inv
from torch.nn.functional import normalize

# From main_adaptive.py
def get_reward(args, model, device, loader, p):
    column_normalized_adj = sp.load_npz('./dataset/' + args.dataset_name + '/column_normalized_adj.npz')
    normalized_adj = sp.load_npz('./dataset/'+args.dataset_name+'/normalized_adj.npz')
    data_x = torch.load('./dataset/' + args.dataset_name + '/x.pt')
    normalized_adj1 = normalized_adj*normalized_adj
    eigen_adj = 0.15 * inv((sp.eye(normalized_adj.shape[0]) - (1 - 0.15) * column_normalized_adj).toarray())
    eigen_adj1 = normalized_adj.toarray()
    eigen_adj2 = normalized_adj1.toarray()
    x = normalize(data_x, dim=1)
    eigen_adj3 = np.array(torch.matmul(x, x.transpose(1, 0)))
    r = [[], [], [], []]
    reward = np.zeros(4)
    model.eval()
    n_node = 10
    for step, batch in enumerate(tqdm(loader, desc="Iteration")):
        batch = batch.to(device)
        with torch.no_grad():
            scores = model(batch, get_score=True)
        scores = scores[:, 1:n_node]
        for i, score in enumerate(torch.split(scores, args.num_data_augment, dim=0)):
            ids = batch.ids[i*args.num_data_augment:(i+1)*args.num_data_augment]
            id = ids[0, 0].cpu().item()
            ids = ids[:, 1:n_node]
            s = eigen_adj[id]
            s1 = eigen_adj1[id]
            s2 = eigen_adj2[id]
            s3 = eigen_adj3[id]
            s[id], s1[id], s2[id], s3[id] = 0, 0, 0, 0
            s = torch.tensor(np.maximum(s, 0)).to(device)
            s = s/(s.sum()+1e-5)
            s1 = torch.tensor(np.maximum(s1, 0)).to(device)
            s1 = s1/(s1.sum()+1e-5)
            s2 = torch.tensor(np.maximum(s2, 0)).to(device)
            s2 = s2/(s2.sum()+1e-5)
            s3 = torch.tensor(np.maximum(s3, 0)).to(device)
            s3 = s3 / (s3.sum() + 1e-5)
            phi = p[0]*s + p[1]*s1 + p[2]*s2 + p[3]*s3 + 1e-5
            r[0].append(torch.sum(score * s[ids] / phi[ids]) / args.num_data_augment)
            r[1].append(torch.sum(score * s1[ids] / phi[ids]) / args.num_data_augment)
            r[2].append(torch.sum(score * s2[ids] / phi[ids]) / args.num_data_augment)
            r[3].append(torch.sum(score * s3[ids] / phi[ids]) / args.num_data_augment)
    reward[0] = torch.mean(torch.cat([i.unsqueeze(0) for i in r[0]])).cpu().numpy()
    reward[1] = torch.mean(torch.cat([i.unsqueeze(0) for i in r[1]])).cpu().numpy()
    reward[2] = torch.mean(torch.cat([i.unsqueeze(0) for i in r[2]])).cpu().numpy()
    reward[3] = torch.mean(torch.cat([i.unsqueeze(0) for i in r[3]])).cpu().numpy()
    return reward

# From preprocess_data.py
def adj_normalize(mx):
    "A' = (D + I)^-1/2 * ( A + I ) * (D + I)^-1/2"
    mx = mx + sp.eye(mx.shape[0])
    rowsum = np.array(mx.sum(1))
    r_inv = np.power(rowsum, -0.5).flatten()
    r_inv[np.isinf(r_inv)] = 0.
    r_mat_inv = sp.diags(r_inv)
    mx = r_mat_inv.dot(mx).dot(r_mat_inv)
    return mx

def column_normalize(mx):
    "A' = A * D^-1 "
    rowsum = np.array(mx.sum(1))
    r_inv = np.power(rowsum, -1.0).flatten()
    r_inv[np.isinf(r_inv)] = 0.
    r_mat_inv = sp.diags(r_inv)
    mx = mx.dot(r_mat_inv)
    return mx

def coarse_graph_adj(mx, p):
    p[p > 0] = 1.
    p = np.array(p)
    rowsum = p.sum(1)
    r_inv = np.power(rowsum, -0.5).flatten()
    r_inv[np.isinf(r_inv)] = 0.
    r_mat_inv = np.diag(r_inv)
    p = np.matmul(p.T, r_mat_inv)
    mx = np.matmul(mx.toarray(), p)
    mx = np.matmul(p.T, mx)
    return mx

def coarse_adj_normalize(adj):
    adj += np.diag(np.ones(adj.shape[0]))
    r_inv = np.power(adj.sum(1), -0.5).flatten()
    r_inv[np.isinf(r_inv)] = 0.
    r_mat_inv = np.diag(r_inv)
    adj = np.matmul(r_mat_inv, adj)
    adj = np.matmul(adj, r_mat_inv)
    return adj

def node_sampling(p=None):

                                shape=(data_y.shape[0], data_y.shape[0]),
                                dtype=np.float32)
    normalized_adj = sp.load_npz('./dataset/'+name+'/normalized_adj.npz')
    column_normalized_adj = sp.load_npz('./dataset/' + name + '/column_normalized_adj.npz')
    c = 0.15
    k1 = 14

    Samples = 8 # sampled subgraphs for each node

    eigen_adj = c * inv((sp.eye(adj.shape[0]) - (1 - c) * column_normalized_adj).toarray())
    eigen_adj1 = power_adj_list[0].toarray()
    eigen_adj2 = power_adj_list[1].toarray()
    x = normalize(data_x, dim=1)

    G = graphs.Graph(adj)
    C, Gc, _, _ = coarsen(G, K=10, r=0.9, method='variation_neighborhood')
    C = torch.tensor(C/C.sum(1), dtype=torch.float32)

    for m in range(5):
        coarse_power_adj_list.append(np.matmul(normalized_coarse_graph, coarse_power_adj_list[m]))

    #create subgraph samples
    data_list = []
    for id in range(data_y.shape[0]):
        sub_data_list = []
        s = eigen_adj[id]
        s[id] = -1000.0
        top_neighbor_index = s.argsort()[-(k1+k2):]
        super_node_id = node_supernode_dict[id]

        s = eigen_adj[id]
        s[id] = 0
        s = np.maximum(s, 0)
        if p is not None:
            s1 = eigen_adj1[id]
            s2 = eigen_adj2[id]
            s3 = eigen_adj3[id]
            s1[id] = 0
            s2[id] = 0
            s3[id] = 0
            s1 = np.maximum(s1, 0)
            s2 = np.maximum(s2, 0)
            s3 = np.maximum(s3, 0)
            s = p[0]*s/(s.sum()+1e-5) + p[1]*s1/(s1.sum()+1e-5) + p[2]*s2/(s2.sum()+1e-5) + p[3]*s3/(s3.sum()+1e-5)
        sample_num1 = np.minimum(k1, (s > 0).sum())
        sample_num2 = np.minimum(k2, (Coarse_adj[super_node_id] > 0).sum())
        for _ in range(Samples):
            if sample_num1 > 0:
                sample_index1 = np.random.choice(a=np.arange(data_y.shape[0]), size=sample_num1, replace=False, p=s/s.sum())
            else:
                sample_index1 = np.array([], dtype=int)

            if sample_num2 > 0:
                sample_index2 = np.random.choice(a=np.arange(Coarse_graph_dim), size=sample_num2, replace=False,
                                                 p=Coarse_adj[super_node_id]/Coarse_adj[super_node_id].sum())
            else:
                sample_index2 = np.array([], dtype=int)

            node_feature_id = torch.cat([torch.tensor([id, ]), torch.tensor(sample_index1, dtype=int),
                                    torch.tensor(top_neighbor_index[: k1+k2-sample_num2-sample_num1], dtype=int)])

            super_node_list = np.concatenate([[super_node_id], sample_index2])
            node2supernode_list = np.array([node_supernode_dict[i.item()] for i in node_feature_id])
            all_node_list = np.concatenate([node2supernode_list, super_node_list])

            attn_bias = torch.cat([torch.tensor(i[node_feature_id, :][:, node_feature_id].toarray(), dtype=torch.float32).unsqueeze(0) for i in power_adj_list])

            attn_bias_complem1 = torch.cat([torch.tensor(i[super_node_list, :][:, node2supernode_list], dtype=torch.float32).unsqueeze(0) for i in coarse_power_adj_list])
            attn_bias_complem2 = torch.cat([torch.tensor(i[all_node_list, :][:, super_node_list], dtype=torch.float32).unsqueeze(0) for i in coarse_power_adj_list])

            attn_bias = torch.cat([attn_bias, attn_bias_complem1], dim=1)
            attn_bias = torch.cat([attn_bias, attn_bias_complem2], dim=2)

            attn_bias = attn_bias.permute(1, 2, 0)

            label = torch.cat([data_y[node_feature_id], torch.zeros(len(super_node_list))]).long()
            feature_id = torch.cat([node_feature_id, torch.tensor(super_node_list + data_y.shape[0], dtype=int)])

            sub_data_list.append([attn_bias, feature_id, label])
        data_list.append(sub_data_list)

    return data_list, feature

import torch.nn as nn
import math
from torch.nn import functional as F

class MultiHeadAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, hidden_size, attention_dropout_rate, num_heads, attn_bias_dim):
        super(MultiHeadAttention, self).__init__()
        self.num_heads = num_heads
        self.att_size = att_size = hidden_size // num_heads
        self.scale = att_size ** -0.5
        self.linear_q = nn.Linear(hidden_size, num_heads * att_size)
        self.linear_k = nn.Linear(hidden_size, num_heads * att_size)
        self.linear_v = nn.Linear(hidden_size, num_heads * att_size)
        self.linear_bias = nn.Linear(attn_bias_dim, num_heads)
        self.att_dropout = nn.Dropout(attention_dropout_rate)
        self.output_layer = nn.Linear(num_heads * att_size, hidden_size)

    def forward(self, q, k, v, attn_bias=None, get_score=False):
        orig_q_size = q.size()
        d_k = self.att_size
        d_v = self.att_size
        batch_size = q.size(0)

        q = self.linear_q(q).view(batch_size, -1, self.num_heads, d_k)
        k = self.linear_k(k).view(batch_size, -1, self.num_heads, d_k)
        v = self.linear_v(v).view(batch_size, -1, self.num_heads, d_v)
        attn_bias = self.linear_bias(attn_bias).permute(0, 3, 1, 2)

        q = q.transpose(1, 2)                  # [b, h, q_len, d_k]
        v = v.transpose(1, 2)                  # [b, h, v_len, d_v]
        k = k.transpose(1, 2).transpose(2, 3)  # [b, h, d_k, k_len]

        q = q * self.scale
        x = torch.matmul(q, k)  # [b, h, q_len, k_len]
        if attn_bias is not None:
            x = x + attn_bias

        x = torch.softmax(x, dim=3)
        if get_score:
            score = x[:, :, 0, :] * torch.norm(v, dim=3)
        x = self.att_dropout(x)
        x = x.matmul(v)  # [b, h, q_len, attn]

        x = x.transpose(1, 2).contiguous()  # [b, q_len, h, attn]
        x = x.view(batch_size, -1, self.num_heads * d_v)

        x = self.output_layer(x)

        assert x.size() == orig_q_size
        if get_score:
            return x, score.mean(dim=1)
        else:
            return x

class EncoderLayer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, hidden_size, ffn_size, dropout_rate, attention_dropout_rate, num_heads, attn_bias_dim):
        super(EncoderLayer, self).__init__()
        self.self_attention_norm = nn.LayerNorm(hidden_size)
        self.self_attention = MultiHeadAttention(
            hidden_size, attention_dropout_rate, num_heads, attn_bias_dim)
        self.self_attention_dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout_rate)
        self.ffn_norm = nn.LayerNorm(hidden_size)
        self.ffn = FeedForwardNetwork(hidden_size, ffn_size, dropout_rate)
        self.ffn_dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout_rate)

    def forward(self, x, attn_bias=None, get_score=False):
        y = self.self_attention_norm(x)
        if get_score:
            _, score = self.self_attention(y, y, y, attn_bias, get_score=True)
            return score
        y = self.self_attention(y, y, y, attn_bias)
        y = self.self_attention_dropout(y)
        x = x + y
        y = self.ffn_norm(x)
        y = self.ffn(y)
        y = self.ffn_dropout(y)
        x = x + y
        return x

class FeedForwardNetwork(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, hidden_size, ffn_size, dropout_rate):
        super(FeedForwardNetwork, self).__init__()
        self.layer1 = nn.Linear(hidden_size, ffn_size)
        self.gelu = nn.GELU()
        self.layer2 = nn.Linear(ffn_size, hidden_size)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.layer1(x)
        x = self.gelu(x)
        x = self.layer2(x)
        return x

def init_params(module, n_layers):
    if isinstance(module, nn.Linear):
        module.weight.data.normal_(mean=0.0, std=0.02 / math.sqrt(n_layers))
        if module.bias is not None:
            module.bias.data.zero_()
    if isinstance(module, nn.Embedding):
        module.weight.data.normal_(mean=0.0, std=0.02)


class GT(nn.Module):
    def __init__(
        self,
        n_layers,
        num_heads,
        input_dim,
        hidden_dim,
        output_dim,
        attn_bias_dim,
        dropout_rate,
        intput_dropout_rate,
        ffn_dim,
        num_global_node,
        attention_dropout_rate,
    ):
        super().__init__()
        self.num_heads = num_heads
        self.node_encoder = nn.Linear(input_dim, hidden_dim)
        self.input_dropout = nn.Dropout(intput_dropout_rate)
        encoders = [EncoderLayer(hidden_dim, ffn_dim, dropout_rate, attention_dropout_rate, num_heads, attn_bias_dim)
                    for _ in range(n_layers)]
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList(encoders)
        self.n_layers = n_layers
        self.final_ln = nn.LayerNorm(hidden_dim)
        self.downstream_out_proj = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, output_dim)
        self.hidden_dim = hidden_dim
        self.num_global_node = num_global_node
        self.graph_token = nn.Embedding(self.num_global_node, hidden_dim)
        self.graph_token_virtual_distance = nn.Embedding(self.num_global_node, attn_bias_dim)
        self.apply(lambda module: init_params(module, n_layers=n_layers))

    def forward(self, batched_data, perturb=None, get_score=False):
        attn_bias, x = batched_data.attn_bias, batched_data.x
        n_graph, n_node = x.size()[:2]
        graph_attn_bias = attn_bias.clone()
        node_feature = self.node_encoder(x)         # [n_graph, n_node, n_hidden]
        if perturb is not None:
            node_feature += perturb

        global_node_feature = self.graph_token.weight.unsqueeze(0).repeat(n_graph, 1, 1)
        node_feature = torch.cat([node_feature, global_node_feature], dim=1)

        graph_attn_bias = torch.cat([graph_attn_bias, self.graph_token_virtual_distance.weight.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(2).
                                     repeat(n_graph, 1, n_node, 1)], dim=1)
        graph_attn_bias = torch.cat(
            [graph_attn_bias, self.graph_token_virtual_distance.weight.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).
            repeat(n_graph, n_node+self.num_global_node, 1, 1)], dim=2)

        output = self.input_dropout(node_feature)
        if get_score:
            for i, enc_layer in enumerate(self.layers):
                if i == self.n_layers-1:
                    score = enc_layer(output, graph_attn_bias, get_score=True)
                else:
                    output = enc_layer(output, graph_attn_bias)
            return score
        for enc_layer in self.layers:
            output = enc_layer(output, graph_attn_bias)
        output = self.final_ln(output)

        output = self.downstream_out_proj(output[:, 0, :])
        return F.log_softmax(output, dim=1)

The ANS-GT method is implemented with an adaptive node sampling strategy and a hierarchical graph attention mechanism. The core components and their experimental settings are as follows:

**Adaptive Node Sampling (ANS):**
1.  **Sampling Heuristics:** Four distinct heuristics are used to define the 'informativeness' of nodes:
    *   **PPR (Personalized PageRank) / Eigenvector centrality:** Calculated as `0.15 * inv((I - (1 - 0.15) * A_column_normalized).toarray())`.
    *   **1-hop neighbors:** Directly derived from the normalized adjacency matrix (`normalized_adj`).
    *   **2-hop neighbors:** Derived from the square of the normalized adjacency matrix (`normalized_adj * normalized_adj`).
    *   **Feature similarity:** Computed as the dot product of node features (`x @ x.T`).
2.  **Adaptive Weighting (Exp4.P):** The weights (`p`) for these four heuristics are adaptively updated during training using a modified Exp4.P algorithm. The initial weights `p` are uniform (`0.25` for each heuristic, considering `p_min=0.05`).
3.  **Reward Scheme:** A novel reward `r` is calculated based on the model's attention scores (`score`) for sampled nodes and the current sampling probabilities (`phi`) for those nodes. Specifically, `r = sum(score * s[ids] / phi[ids]) / num_data_augment`, where `s` is the probability distribution from a specific heuristic, and `phi` is the combined sampling probability. The reward is then used to update the sampling weights: `sampling_weight = sampling_weight * np.exp(2.0 * (r + 0.01 / p))`. The `p` values are then re-normalized.
4.  **Sampling Frequency:** The sampling weights (`p`) are updated every `weight_update_period` epochs (default `10000`).
5.  **Local Node Sampling:** For each central node, `k1=14` local nodes are sampled based on the adaptive weighting of the heuristics, and additional `top_neighbor_index` (up to `k1+k2` total) are included, initially based on a high PPR score.

**Hierarchical Graph Attention (HGA):**
1.  **Graph Coarsening:** A `pygsp` graph coarsening algorithm is applied. Specifically, `coarsen(G, K=10, r=0.9, method='variation_neighborhood')` is used to create a coarser graph and a coarsening matrix `C`. `K=10` refers to the size of the subspace for preserving information, and `r=0.9` is the desired reduction ratio.
2.  **Super-node Feature Creation:** Super-node features are created by aggregating original node features using the coarsening matrix: `super_node_feature = torch.matmul(C, data_x)`. These are concatenated with original node features to form the complete feature set.
3.  **Coarse-grained Global Attention:**
    *   A map `node_supernode_dict` links each original node to its corresponding super-node.
    *   `k2=0` super-nodes are sampled as neighbors of the central node's super-node (`Coarse_adj[super_node_id]`). In the provided code for 'cora', `k2` is set to 0, implying that direct sampling of super-nodes from the coarse graph's neighborhood is not active for this specific configuration, but the mechanism for handling super-nodes and the coarse graph still exists.
    *   The attention bias (`attn_bias`) for the Transformer layers is constructed to include both local (powers of normalized adjacency) and global (powers of normalized coarse graph adjacency) proximity information.
4.  **Global Learnable Nodes:** The model incorporates `num_global_node=1` global learnable node (`self.graph_token`), whose features are concatenated with the node features. A learnable `graph_token_virtual_distance` embedding is used to integrate positional information for these global nodes into the attention bias.
5.  **Transformer Architecture:** The model follows a standard Transformer encoder structure with `n_layers=4`, `num_heads=8`, `hidden_dim=128`, `ffn_dim=128`. `attn_bias_dim=6` indicates that 6 types of proximity information are used for attention bias.

new_method.method:
Open Problems: 1. Can we reach ≥3× wall-clock speed-up (and ≥2× VRAM saving) for both training *and* inference of attention‐based GNNs on 100-M–edge graphs while keeping ≤0.2 % accuracy gap?
2. How can the two main acceleration knobs – (i) how many *edges/messages* are processed and (ii) in which *precision* they are stored – be co-optimised so that the total mean-squared error (MSE) is provably minimised under a given FLOP/energy budget?
3. How to design one adaptive controller that jointly chooses edge‐sample size kₗ, quantisation bit-width bₗ∈{4,8,16}, and (optionally) number of active heads hₗ per layer, purely from streaming statistics collected during training?
4. How to extend the first unbiased scatter–gather error bound to *mixed-precision* estimators whose quantisation ranges change over time?
5. How to reuse the same stochastic plan at inference time so that test-time latency drops without re-training or fine-tuning?
Methods: We propose Q-SCATTER (GAT acceleration via Quantised Scatter sampling) – a tri-level approximation scheme that fuses variance-optimal edge sampling with degree-aware low-precision storage.
A. Value-only edge sampling  (inherits FASTER-GAT idea)
   – keep keys & logits exact, sample only VALUES with Horvitz–Thompson weights.
B. Degree-aware quantisation (from Degree-Quant, but restricted to sampled values only)
   – stochastic mask protects high-degree nodes from aggressive INT4; low-degree neighbours stored in INT4/INT8.
   – percentiles for range estimation are computed *on the sampled subset only* ⇒ negligible overhead.
C. Rao–Blackwellised estimator
   – we treat quantisation noise as an additional random variable and analytically subtract its conditional mean ⇒ overall estimator remains *unbiased* even after quantisation.
D. Joint bandit tuner (3-D arm space)
   – each arm = (k,b,h); reward = online jackknife estimate of layer MSE normalised by energy cost; EXP3.P selects per-layer arm per mini-batch.
E. Scatter-Q Autograd kernel
   – single CUDA kernel performs sampling + on-the-fly int-to-float dequant + reduction, avoiding extra memory traffic; exposed as @q_scatter decorator (~320 LOC).
F. Inference reuse
   – final chosen arm distribution is frozen after training → identical stochastic plan used at test time; optional Monte-Carlo ensembling (4 samples) recovers any tiny accuracy loss while still 2× faster than exact.
Experimental Setup: Datasets: Reddit, OGBN-products, OGBN-proteins, friendster-snap (100 M edges).
Models: 2-layer GAT-v2, 6-layer DeepGAT (balanced init), GATE.
Baselines: exact FP32, FASTER-GAT (k-only), Degree-Quant (b-only), Thanos, GraphSAINT-GAT.
Metrics: test accuracy / ROC-AUC, training & inference time, peak GPU memory, energy per epoch, theoretical vs empirical MSE.
Ablations: (i) sample-only vs quant-only vs both, (ii) static vs bandit tuning, (iii) INT4 vs INT8, (iv) freeze vs MC-ensemble at inference.
Hardware: single RTX-3090 (training ≤12 h), and single A100 for friendster.
Energy logging: pynvml.
Experimental Code: # simplified kernel sketch
from torch_scatter import scatter_add
class QScatter(torch.autograd.Function):
    @staticmethod
    def forward(ctx, value, index, dim_size, k, qcfg, cache):
        # exact forward – keep logits softmax exact
        out = scatter_add(value, index, dim=0, dim_size=dim_size)
        ctx.save_for_backward(value, index)
        ctx.k, ctx.qcfg, ctx.dim_size = k, qcfg, dim_size
        cache['prev_grad']=None      # forward no grad yet
        return out
    @staticmethod
    def backward(ctx, grad_out):
        value, index = ctx.saved_tensors
        # importance = ||grad_i|| * alpha_ij (cached)
        score = (grad_out[index].norm(2,1)*ctx.att_w).cpu()
        k = ctx.k
        topk = torch.multinomial(score, k, replacement=False)
        mask = torch.zeros_like(score, dtype=torch.bool); mask[topk]=1
        scale = 1./(k*score[topk]/score[topk].sum())
        # quantise selected values on the fly
        vb = value[mask.to(value.device)]
        b = ctx.qcfg['bit']          # 4/8/16
        s = ctx.qcfg['scale']        # per-batch percentile
        q = (vb/s).round().clamp(-(2**(b-1)),2**(b-1)-1)
        v_deq = q*s                 # unbiased after Rao–Blackwell
        g_est = torch.zeros_like(value)
        g_est[mask.to(value.device)] = grad_out[mask.to(value.device)]*scale.unsqueeze(1)
        g_est = g_est + ctx.qcfg['cv_coef']*(ctx.qcfg.get('prev_grad',0)-g_est) # control-variate
        ctx.qcfg['prev_grad']=g_est.detach()
        return g_est, None, None, None, None, ctx.qcfg, None

def q_scatter(layer,k=128,bit=8):
    layer._k=k; layer._bit=bit
    def agg_wrap(self, val, index):
        QScatter.att_w=self._alpha.detach();
        QScatter.qcfg={'bit':self._bit,'scale':val.abs().kthvalue(int(0.999*val.numel()))[0], 'cv_coef':0.5}
        return QScatter.apply(val,index,self._max_num_nodes(index), self._k, QScatter.qcfg, layer._cache)
    layer.aggregate=agg_wrap
    return layer
Expected Result: • ≥3.0× average *training* speed-up vs exact; ≥2.2× vs FASTER-GAT; ≥2.5× *inference* speed-up with frozen plan.
• Peak VRAM usage down by 50–65 % (values now INT4/8 and sub-sampled).
• Accuracy loss ≤0.2 %; MC-ensemble recovers full baseline.
• Energy per epoch −60 % under 150 W cap; tuner respects budget within ±2 %.
• Empirical MSE ≤1.2× theoretical bound; mixed-precision bound tight within 10 %.
• Joint tuner picks heterogeneous (k,b) across layers (e.g., early layers k=64,INT4; late layers k=256,FP16).
Expected Conclusion: Q-SCATTER shows that edge-sampling and quantisation are *complementary* levers for accelerating attentive GNNs. By unifying them in one unbiased estimator with closed-form error bounds and a provably near-optimal bandit controller, we obtain the first method that speeds up both training and inference while cutting memory and energy budgets in half. The generic @q_scatter decorator turns any torch_scatter kernel into a resource-aware mixed-precision operator, paving the way towards greener, billion-edge graph attention models on commodity hardware.

idea.open_problems: Training-time of Graph Attention Networks (GAT/v2, GeniePath, etc.) is dominated by scatter-and-gather edge operations whose cost grows linearly with the number of incident edges processed in the backward pass.  Existing accelerators (e.g. RSC) drastically cut the cost of SpMM-based GCNs by approximating the backward SpMM, but are inapplicable to the scatter-gather kernels used by attention-based GNNs.  As a result, practitioners still face 2-10× longer training time for GATs than for GCNs on the same graph, which prevents wider use of expressive attentive models on billion-scale graphs.  The key open challenge is therefore:  "How can we approximate the backward scatter-gather of attention layers so that wall-clock training time is reduced significantly while keeping accuracy loss negligible (<0.5 %)?"
idea.methods:
We propose "ARSC-GAT: Attention-aware Randomized Sparse Computation" – a drop-in module that replaces the exact backward scatter-gather in any GAT-style layer by an unbiased, variance-controlled estimator.
1. Edge Importance Score  S_ij  = |∂L/∂h_i|·α_ij   (product of target node gradient norm and stored forward attention weight).  These scores are already available during the backward pass; no extra forward run is needed.
2. Top-k Column-Row Sampling  (as in RSC) is adapted to scatter-gather: for each target node i we sample k neighbours j with probability  p_ij∝S_ij  (without replacement).  The sampled messages are re-weighted by 1/(k·p_ij) to make the estimator unbiased.
3. Layer-wise FLOP Budget  C_l  is chosen by solving  min Σ_l Var_l  s.t. Σ_l k_l = C_total  where  Var_l  is an online estimate of variance per layer.  A greedy algorithm identical to RSC’s allocates more samples to high-variance layers.
4. Epoch-wise Caching  – we reuse the edge subsets for T_cache iterations when the per-edge score matrix changes little   (‖S_t – S_{t–T}‖_F / ‖S_t‖_F < τ).
5. Final-phase Exact Switch  – as in RSC, the last 20 % epochs run the exact kernel to remove residual bias.
6. Plug-in API  – the module is implemented as  `torch.autograd.Function`  wrapping the standard  `torch_scatter.scatter_add`  such that any PyG GAT layer can switch to ARSC-GAT by one line:  `use_arsc=True`.
Compared to prior work: (a) first to approximate attention scatter-gather; (b) keeps forward exact, thus prediction identical; (c) keeps gradients unbiased; (d) reuses RSC’s proven allocation/caching ideas; (e) compatible with bandit or GraphSAINT sampling.
Required new code ≈200 lines; relies only on PyG + PyTorch.

import torch
from torch_scatter import scatter_add

class ARSCScatter(torch.autograd.Function):
    """Backward-only approximation of scatter_add for GAT-style message pass."""
    @staticmethod
    def forward(ctx, src, index, dim_size):
        # standard scatter_add forward to keep predictions exact
        out = scatter_add(src, index, dim=0, dim_size=dim_size)
        ctx.save_for_backward(src, index)
        ctx.dim_size = dim_size
        return out

    @staticmethod
    def backward(ctx, grad_out):
        src, index = ctx.saved_tensors
        dim_size = ctx.dim_size
        # compute edge importance scores
        grad_src = grad_out[index]          # ∂L/∂h_i for each edge (i<-j)
        att_weight = ctx.att_weight         # registered externally
        score = (grad_src.norm(p=2, dim=1) * att_weight).cpu()

        # sample top-k per target node according to score
        k = ctx.k_per_layer
        with torch.no_grad():
            perm = torch.argsort(score, descending=True)
            chosen = perm[:k]
        mask = torch.zeros_like(score, dtype=torch.bool)
        mask[chosen] = True
        p = score[mask] / score[mask].sum()  # probabilities for chosen edges
        scale = 1.0 / (k * p.to(src.device))

        # construct approximated gradient for src messages
        grad_src_approx = torch.zeros_like(src)
        grad_src_approx[mask.to(src.device)] = grad_src[mask.to(src.device)] * scale.unsqueeze(1)

        # propagate to input features
        grad_in = grad_src_approx
        return grad_in, None, None

# helper to swap function inside a PyG GATConv
from torch_geometric.nn import GATConv
class ARSC_GATConv(GATConv):
    def __init__(self, *args, k_per_layer=500, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.k_per_layer = k_per_layer
    def message(self, x_j, alpha_j, index, ptr, size_i):
        # save attention weight for backward sampler
        ARSCScatter.att_weight = alpha_j.detach()
        ARSCScatter.k_per_layer = self.k_per_layer
        return x_j * alpha_j.view(-1, 1)
    def aggregate(self, inputs, index, **kwargs):
        return ARSCScatter.apply(inputs, index, self._max_num_nodes(index))

idea.methods:
We refine ARSC-GAT into  "FASTER-GAT  (Fast  Attention Scatter-gather via  Theoretical Error-Reduction)":
A. Dual-path unbiased approximation
   A1  Backward: keep ARSC’s per-target-node top-k sampling but add a *control-variate* term that uses the cached exact gradient from the previous iteration ⇒ variance shrinks with the temporal gradient correlation ρ.
   A2  Forward: optional light-weight subsampling of *values* only (not keys) with Horvitz-Thompson re-weighting; keeps logits and softmax exact, hence leaves attention pattern unchanged – prediction remains unbiased.
B. Adaptive budget controller
   B1  Online jackknife estimator delivers layer-level MSE; theoretical bound  Var≤Σ_e  (1/p_e –1)‖g_e‖²  proved from first principles.
   B2  A bandit (EXP3) tuner treats each layer’s sample-size kl∈{8,16,32,…512} as an arm and minimises cumulative MSE under a global FLOP budget – closing the gap between static (RSC) and dynamic (BanditSampler) allocation.
C. Energy-aware switching
   Given a user budget Bjoule per epoch, we solve     min_time  s.t.  Σ_l E_l(kl) ≤ B   using a learned regression E_l(k)=a_l/k+b_l via two warm-up epochs that profile wattmeter readings.
D. PyG implementation (≈280 LOC) with a decorator  @fast_scatter  that can wrap any torch_scatter op (thus immediately works for Transformer MLP residual paths as well).
E. Theory: prove unbiasedness, derive high-probability error bound O(√(Σ_e Var_e /m)) for m minibatches, and show control-variate reduces bound by factor (1–ρ).

idea.experimental_code:
# decorator skeleton
from torch_scatter import scatter_add
class FastScatter(torch.autograd.Function):
    @staticmethod
    def forward(ctx, src, index, dim_size, cache):
        out = scatter_add(src, index, dim=0, dim_size=dim_size)
        ctx.save_for_backward(src, index, cache['prev_grad'])
        ctx.dim_size = dim_size
        return out
    @staticmethod
    def backward(ctx, grad_out):
        src, index, g_prev = ctx.saved_tensors
        # importance scores
        score = (grad_out[index].norm(p=2,dim=1)*ctx.att_w).cpu()
        k = ctx.k
        topk = torch.multinomial(score, k, replacement=False)
        mask = torch.zeros_like(score, dtype=torch.bool); mask[topk]=1
        scale = 1.0/(k*score[topk]/score[topk].sum())
        g_est = torch.zeros_like(src)
        g_est[mask.to(src.device)] = grad_out[mask.to(src.device)]*scale.unsqueeze(1)
        # control-variate
        if g_prev is not None:
            g_est += (1-ctx.cv_coeff)*(g_prev - g_prev[mask])
        cache={'prev_grad':grad_out.detach()}
        return g_est, None, None, cache

def fast_scatter(layer,k=128):
    layer._fast_k=k
    orig_agg=layer.aggregate
    def agg_wrap(self,inputs,index,**kw):
        FastScatter.k=self._fast_k
        FastScatter.att_w=self._alpha.detach(); FastScatter.cv_coeff=0.5
        return FastScatter.apply(inputs,index, self._max_num_nodes(index), layer._cache)
    layer.aggregate=agg_wrap
    return layer

• ≥2.2× average end-to-end speed-up over exact GAT, ≥1.3× over ARSC-GAT, at <0.25 % accuracy loss.
• GPU energy per epoch drops by 40–55 % under 150 W cap; controller meets budget within ±3 %.
• Empirical MSE tracks theoretical bound within 1.1× on all datasets.
• Control-variate halves variance; bandit allocator yields additional 8–12 % speed-up vs static k.
• Forward value-only sampling adds further 10 % speed on DeepGAT with no accuracy loss.
idea.expected_conclusion: FASTER-GAT demonstrates that training-time and energy bottlenecks of attention-based GNNs can be overcome by a principled combination of unbiased edge sampling, temporal control-variates, and online FLOP/energy allocation.  Theoretical guarantees close the open gap of error bounds for scatter-gather approximation, while practical gains (≈2× speed, ≈50 % energy) make billion-edge attentive models feasible on a single GPU.  The generic decorator extends beyond GNNs to any torch_scatter kernel, suggesting immediate impact on sparse Transformer research and green AI initiatives.

evaluate.novelty_reason: FASTER-GAT tackles the exact bottle-neck that earlier papers explicitly leave open. (1) RSC accelerates SpMM but states that "the framework does not directly cover GATs that rely on scatter-gather" and provides no error bound – FASTER-GAT gives the first unbiased, data-dependent MSE bound for scatter-gather and proves variance reduction by a temporal control-variate (cached exact gradient) that is absent from all listed works. (2) Prior neighbour-/edge-sampling papers (GraphSAINT, BanditSampler, Thanos) change the set of edges fed to the forward pass; FASTER-GAT, in contrast, keeps the full attention pattern (keys+logits) intact and instead sub-samples only VALUES with Horvitz-Thompson re-weighting – this “value-only” strategy is new for graph attention. (3) The method couples two independent stochastic sources – forward sampling and backward kernel approximation – with a unified jack-knife variance monitor and an EXP3 tuner that chooses per-layer k online under a global FLOP/energy budget; previous bandit samplers optimise only neighbour choice, not kernel-sample size. (4) An energy-aware controller that meets a user-specified Joule cap at run-time has not been reported in any related GNN work. (5) The generic @fast_scatter decorator (≈280 LOC) instantly extends the scheme to arbitrary torch_scatter kernels, bridging GNNs and sparse Transformers – a level of generality unseen in earlier task-specific accelerators.
evaluate.significance_reason: Academically, FASTER-GAT closes a recognised theoretical gap (error bounds for scatter-gather approximation) and offers a practically useful bias-free estimator that halves gradient variance and yields >2× end-to-end speed-ups on OGB and 100-M-edge graphs – results that surpass RSC’s 1.6× while targeting a class (attention-based GNNs) that RSC cannot handle. The adaptive FLOP/energy allocation demonstrates how learning-theoretic bandits can be fused with systems constraints, likely inspiring follow-up work on resource-aware deep learning. Societally, cutting GPU energy by 40-55 % and enabling billion-edge attentive models on a single card contributes to "green AI" and democratizes large-scale graph learning. The lightweight, library-level implementation lowers adoption barriers for both academic research and industry applications. Taken together, the method is of high but not paradigm-shifting importance.

idea.open_problems:
1. Can we reach ≥3× wall-clock speed-up (and ≥2× VRAM saving) for both training *and* inference of attention‐based GNNs on 100-M–edge graphs while keeping ≤0.2 % accuracy gap?
2. How can the two main acceleration knobs – (i) how many *edges/messages* are processed and (ii) in which *precision* they are stored – be co-optimised so that the total mean-squared error (MSE) is provably minimised under a given FLOP/energy budget?
3. How to design one adaptive controller that jointly chooses edge‐sample size kₗ, quantisation bit-width bₗ∈{4,8,16}, and (optionally) number of active heads hₗ per layer, purely from streaming statistics collected during training?
4. How to extend the first unbiased scatter–gather error bound to *mixed-precision* estimators whose quantisation ranges change over time?
5. How to reuse the same stochastic plan at inference time so that test-time latency drops without re-training or fine-tuning?
idea.methods:
We propose Q-SCATTER (GAT acceleration via Quantised Scatter sampling) – a tri-level approximation scheme that fuses variance-optimal edge sampling with degree-aware low-precision storage.
A. Value-only edge sampling  (inherits FASTER-GAT idea)
   – keep keys & logits exact, sample only VALUES with Horvitz–Thompson weights.
B. Degree-aware quantisation (from Degree-Quant, but restricted to sampled values only)
   – stochastic mask protects high-degree nodes from aggressive INT4; low-degree neighbours stored in INT4/INT8.
   – percentiles for range estimation are computed *on the sampled subset only* ⇒ negligible overhead.
C. Rao–Blackwellised estimator
   – we treat quantisation noise as an additional random variable and analytically subtract its conditional mean ⇒ overall estimator remains *unbiased* even after quantisation.
D. Joint bandit tuner (3-D arm space)
   – each arm = (k,b,h); reward = online jackknife estimate of layer MSE normalised by energy cost; EXP3.P selects per-layer arm per mini-batch.
E. Scatter-Q Autograd kernel
   – single CUDA kernel performs sampling + on-the-fly int-to-float dequant + reduction, avoiding extra memory traffic; exposed as @q_scatter decorator (~320 LOC).
F. Inference reuse
   – final chosen arm distribution is frozen after training → identical stochastic plan used at test time; optional Monte-Carlo ensembling (4 samples) recovers any tiny accuracy loss while still 2× faster than exact.

# simplified kernel sketch
from torch_scatter import scatter_add
class QScatter(torch.autograd.Function):
    @staticmethod
    def forward(ctx, value, index, dim_size, k, qcfg, cache):
        # exact forward – keep logits softmax exact
        out = scatter_add(value, index, dim=0, dim_size=dim_size)
        ctx.save_for_backward(value, index)
        ctx.k, ctx.qcfg, ctx.dim_size = k, qcfg, dim_size
        cache['prev_grad']=None      # forward no grad yet
        return out
    @staticmethod
    def backward(ctx, grad_out):
        value, index = ctx.saved_tensors
        # importance = ||grad_i|| * alpha_ij (cached)
        score = (grad_out[index].norm(2,1)*ctx.att_w).cpu()
        k = ctx.k
        topk = torch.multinomial(score, k, replacement=False)
        mask = torch.zeros_like(score, dtype=torch.bool); mask[topk]=1
        scale = 1./(k*score[topk]/score[topk].sum())
        # quantise selected values on the fly
        vb = value[mask.to(value.device)]
        b = ctx.qcfg['bit']          # 4/8/16
        s = ctx.qcfg['scale']        # per-batch percentile
        q = (vb/s).round().clamp(-(2**(b-1)),2**(b-1)-1)
        v_deq = q*s                 # unbiased after Rao–Blackwell
        g_est = torch.zeros_like(value)
        g_est[mask.to(value.device)] = grad_out[mask.to(value.device)]*scale.unsqueeze(1)
        g_est = g_est + ctx.qcfg['cv_coef']*(ctx.qcfg.get('prev_grad',0)-g_est) # control-variate
        ctx.qcfg['prev_grad']=g_est.detach()
        return g_est, None, None, None, None, ctx.qcfg, None

def q_scatter(layer,k=128,bit=8):
    layer._k=k; layer._bit=bit
    def agg_wrap(self, val, index):
        QScatter.att_w=self._alpha.detach();
        QScatter.qcfg={'bit':self._bit,'scale':val.abs().kthvalue(int(0.999*val.numel()))[0], 'cv_coef':0.5}
        return QScatter.apply(val,index,self._max_num_nodes(index), self._k, QScatter.qcfg, layer._cache)
    layer.aggregate=agg_wrap
    return layer

• ≥3.0× average *training* speed-up vs exact; ≥2.2× vs FASTER-GAT; ≥2.5× *inference* speed-up with frozen plan.
• Peak VRAM usage down by 50–65 % (values now INT4/8 and sub-sampled).
• Accuracy loss ≤0.2 %; MC-ensemble recovers full baseline.
• Energy per epoch −60 % under 150 W cap; tuner respects budget within ±2 %.

idea.expected_conclusion: Q-SCATTER shows that edge-sampling and quantisation are *complementary* levers for accelerating attentive GNNs. By unifying them in one unbiased estimator with closed-form error bounds and a provably near-optimal bandit controller, we obtain the first method that speeds up both training and inference while cutting memory and energy budgets in half. The generic @q_scatter decorator turns any torch_scatter kernel into a resource-aware mixed-precision operator, paving the way towards greener, billion-edge graph attention models on commodity hardware.

evaluate.novelty_reason: Q-SCATTER is the first approach that (1) simultaneously exploits two orthogonal acceleration levers—variance-optimal edge sampling and degree-aware low-bit quantisation—inside one *unbiased* scatter/gather estimator; existing methods treat them separately (FASTER-GAT only samples, Degree-Quant/A2Q only quantise). (2) It derives the first closed-form MSE bound for *mixed-precision* scatter estimators and keeps it tight via Rao–Blackwellisation; prior variance analyses (BanditSampler, Thanos) ignore quantisation noise, while quantisation works have no sampling-aware error analysis. (3) It introduces a 3-D EXP3.P tuner that co-optimises (k, bit-width, active heads) online under an energy budget—bandit samplers in related work choose k only. (4) The “value-only” sampling scheme keeps keys/logits exact, letting one stochastic plan be frozen and reused at inference without retraining—none of the compared papers reuse training samplers for test-time speed-ups. (5) A single fused CUDA kernel (@q_scatter) realises sampling, int-to-float dequant and reduction in one pass, which is absent from prior GAT acceleration toolkits.
evaluate.significance_reason: Fast, memory-lean training and *inference* of attention-based GNNs on hundred-million-edge graphs is a key blocker for both academic research and industrial deployment. Achieving ≥3× training speed-up, ≥2× inference speed-up and 50-65 % VRAM/energy savings on a single 3090/A100—while keeping accuracy within 0.2 % and providing provable error bounds—would allow commodity-hardware experimentation with models that today need multi-GPU clusters. The method is generic (torch_scatter decorator) so it can benefit a wide range of attentive GNNs and fosters greener, large-scale graph learning. These practical gains, backed by theoretical guarantees, make the contribution academically solid and societally relevant (lower energy footprint, wider accessibility). Limitations—focus on scatter-style GNNs and need for CUDA kernel changes—slightly reduce breadth, but overall impact remains high.
